---
title: "Tutorial: uncertainty of class areas from class probabilities"
execute:
  warning: false
---

Suppose a land-cover model gives a **calibrated probability** for each class in every
cell. Summing those probabilities over a region gives its expected class area. How
uncertain is that area? This mode answers the question per class, following the
continuous method as closely as possible:

- the prediction error is $e_k = I_k - p_k$, with $\sigma_k = \sqrt{p_k(1-p_k)}$;
- one correlogram is fitted per class to the standardized validation errors;
- the variance of the block-fraction error is the same Monte Carlo integral as in the
  continuous case;
- the expected area is $|B|$ times the block mean of $p_k$.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Setup"
import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import shapely

import pyspatialuncertainty as psu
from pyspatialuncertainty.synthetic import LatentClassScenario, SubGridLayout

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.facecolor": "#fcfcfb", "axes.facecolor": "#fcfcfb",
                     "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False, "font.size": 9})
```

## A synthetic class map with known truth

`LatentClassScenario` thresholds a latent Gaussian field into three classes, `forest`,
`grassland` and `wetland`, with overall proportions of about 60 %, 30 % and 10 %. The
latent field is the sum of a known signal μ and spatially correlated noise. Because the
noise distribution is known, the class probabilities given μ are exactly calibrated.

```{python}
sc = LatentClassScenario(layout=SubGridLayout(n=80, cell_size=1.0, f=2),
                         latent=psu.vgm(0.75, "Exp", 6.0, nugget=0.25),
                         classes=("forest", "grassland", "wetland"), n_validation=800)
probs = sc.probabilities()          # DataArray (class, y, x), sums to one
real = sc.simulate(np.random.default_rng(7))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 3.2), constrained_layout=True)
for ax, cls in zip(axes, sc.classes):
    im = ax.imshow(probs.sel({"class": cls}).values, extent=(0, 80, 0, 80), cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=1)
    ax.set_title(f"P({cls})")
fig.colorbar(im, ax=axes, shrink=0.8)
plt.show()
```

## Validating the probabilities

The method needs probabilities that sum to one and are **strictly** between 0 and 1,
because σ_k = sqrt(p(1 − p)) must be positive. Hard zeros or ones are rejected rather than
silently changed:

```{python}
psu.validate_probabilities(probs)            # passes

bad = probs.copy()
bad[:, 0, 0] = [1.0, 0.0, 0.0]
try:
    psu.validate_probabilities(bad)
except psu.ProbabilityError as err:
    print("ProbabilityError:", err)
```

If softening hard probabilities is acceptable for your application, call
`psu.clip_probabilities(p, eps)` explicitly.

## Standardized indicator errors at validation points

The validation table needs the observed class and **out-of-sample** probabilities for
every class at each validation point, for example from cross-validation. Here they come
straight from the calibrated map.

```{python}
cells = real.validation["cell"].to_numpy()
p_flat = probs.values.reshape(3, -1)
val = real.validation.with_columns(
    [pl.Series(f"p_{c}", p_flat[k, cells]) for k, c in enumerate(sc.classes)]
)
errors = psu.indicator_errors(val, {c: f"p_{c}" for c in sc.classes}, label="label")
errors.head()
```

## One correlogram per class

`fit_class_variograms` fits each class with `fit_correlation`. By default this is a
Gaussian likelihood fit with an unknown mean of the errors (REML): the probabilities may
be miscalibrated, and the next step estimates and corrects for that. `method="wls"` gives
the paper's weighted least-squares variogram fit instead. The sample variograms are shown
for checking.

```{python}
fits = psu.fit_class_variograms(errors)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 2.9), constrained_layout=True)
for ax, (cls, cv) in zip(axes, fits.items()):
    ev = cv.empirical
    h = np.linspace(0, ev.cutoff, 150)[1:]
    ax.scatter(ev.dist, ev.gamma, s=ev.n_pairs / 20, color="#2a78d6")
    ax.plot(h, cv.model.gamma(h), color="#2a78d6")
    ax.set_title(f"{cls} (fitted sill {cv.model.sill:.2f})")
    ax.set_xlabel("distance")
plt.show()
```

With calibrated probabilities the standardized errors have unit variance, so the fitted
sills should be near 1. A sill far from 1 is a sign of miscalibration.

## Expected class areas and their uncertainty

The blocks are 20 × 20 tiles plus two polygons. All classes share the same Monte Carlo
point pairs. By default the mean of each class's standardized errors is estimated from
the validation points (held by `fits`), and the block fractions are shifted by it
(`shift`); `mean="zero"` would trust the probabilities' calibration instead.

```{python}
tiles = psu.aggregate_categorical(probs, fits, psu.blocks.tiles(probs, 20), n_mc=10_000, seed=1)
tiles.table.filter(pl.col("block_id") < 2).select(
    "class", "block_id", "map_fraction", "shift", "fraction", "sd_fraction", "lower", "upper", "sd_area")
```

```{python}
pl.DataFrame({"class": list(tiles.mean_estimates),
              "estimated mean of standardized errors": [e.beta for e in tiles.mean_estimates.values()],
              "standard error": [e.se for e in tiles.mean_estimates.values()]})
```

```{python}
ds = tiles.to_xarray(coarse=True)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(10, 6), constrained_layout=True)
for j, cls in enumerate(sc.classes):
    for i, (var, title) in enumerate([("expected_area", "expected area"), ("sd_area", "SD of area")]):
        im = axes[i, j].imshow(ds[var].sel({"class": cls}).values, extent=(0, 80, 0, 80), cmap="viridis")
        axes[i, j].set_title(f"{cls}: {title}")
        fig.colorbar(im, ax=axes[i, j], shrink=0.75)
plt.show()
```

Polygons work the same way. Monte Carlo points are drawn inside the exact geometry:

```{python}
regions = [shapely.Polygon([(5, 5), (60, 10), (40, 50), (8, 40)]), shapely.box(45, 45, 78, 78)]
poly = psu.aggregate_categorical(probs, fits, psu.blocks.polygons(regions, probs, ids=["west", "north-east"]),
                                 n_mc=10_000, seed=2)
poly.table.select("class", "block_id", "area", "expected_area", "sd_area", "area_lower", "area_upper")
```

## How good are these intervals?

Here we know the truth. The latent noise can be simulated again and again, and each time
we can check whether the true block fractions fall inside the 90 % intervals:

```{python}
from pyspatialuncertainty.synthetic import evaluation_blocks

eb = evaluation_blocks(sc.layout, tile_sizes=(20,), max_per_size=16, n_polygons=0)
res = psu.aggregate_categorical(probs, fits, eb.blockset, n_mc=10_000, seed=3)
pred = res.table["fraction"].to_numpy().reshape(3, -1)
sd = res.table["sd_fraction"].to_numpy().reshape(3, -1)
rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
truth = np.array([[eb.block_means(r.fraction_sub[k]) for k in range(3)] for r in (sc.simulate(rng) for _ in range(200))])
covered = np.abs(truth - pred) <= 1.645 * sd
pl.DataFrame({"class": list(sc.classes), "coverage of 90% PI": covered.mean(axis=(0, 2)),
              "estimated SD / simulated SD": (sd / (truth - pred).std(axis=0)).mean(axis=1)})
```

This is a single map and a single correlogram fit. The
[verification report](../report.html) repeats the check over hundreds of realizations,
several block sizes and deliberately miscalibrated probabilities.
